title: Monitor a FastAPI App with Prometheus + Grafana (Metrics, Dashboards, Alerts)
author: Visual Studio Learn
summary: Your FastAPI app is slow, and you cannot see it. There is no graph of your traffic, no counter of your errors, and nothing that tells you which endpoint is the slow one. The first symptom is a user complaint — and by then you are debugging blind. In this tutorial you will fix that, end to end, on your own machine: instrument a FastAPI app so it publishes its own metrics, collect them with Prometheus, and build a Grafana dashboard that catches a slow endpoint live — then set an alert that fires when it happens again. Everything is local and free: no accounts, no API keys, no cloud. What we are using (pinned, so your install matches this post exactly): prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator 8.1.0 · Prometheus 3.16.0 · Grafana OSS 13.3.0 · FastAPI 0.162.4 · uvicorn 0.54.0 · Python 3.12. The complete companion code — the app, the Prometheus config, the load script, the exported dashboard JSON and the alert rule — is in the companion repository , folder topic-10-prometheus-grafana/ . Step 1 — Install the stack Create a virtual environment and install the app stack. The instrumentator is the only monitoring-specific package the app needs: $ python -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate $ pip install fastapi uvicorn prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator Pin what you installed in a requirements.txt ( fastapi==0.162.4 , uvicorn==0.54.0 , prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator==8.1.0 , and httpx==0.28.1 , which the load script in Step 9 uses). Prometheus and Grafana themselves are single binaries you download from their official sites and run locally — no Docker required, which is how this post was produced. Step 2 — The demo app: one endpoint per signal The demo app is deliberately small, with one endpoint per thing a dashboard should show you: import asyncio from fastapi import FastAPI from fastapi . responses import JSONResponse app = FastAPI ( title = "Demo Shop API" ) @app . get ( "/" ) async def home ( ) : # instant JSON — the healthy traffic return { "status" : "ok" , "service" : "demo-shop" } @app . get ( "/slow" ) async def slow ( ) : # sleeps 0.8s, then answers await asyncio . sleep ( 0.8 ) return { "status" : "ok" , "detail" : "that took a while" } @app . get ( "/boom" ) async def boom ( ) : # HTTP 500, every time return JSONResponse ( status_code = 500 , content = { "detail" : "something broke" } ) That file is complete and runnable as written — it is the companion repo's app.py minus the two monitoring lines, which are Step 3. Run it with uvicorn app:app --port 8000 and curl all three: / answers instantly, /slow takes 0.80s on the timer, and /boom returns a clean HTTP 500. Nothing is monitored yet — that is the point. We are about to watch all three behaviours appear on a dashboard. Step 3 — Instrument the app (two calls) This is the whole integration. Add the import and one line after you create the app: from prometheus_fastapi_instrumentator import Instrumentator Instrumentator ( ) . instrument ( app ) . expose ( app ) instrument(app) wraps your app so every request is measured; expose(app) serves those measurements at a new endpoint, /metrics . Restart uvicorn, generate a few requests, and open http://localhost:8000/metrics in your browser. Step 4 — Read what /metrics gives you for free Without writing a single metric yourself, the instrumentator publishes five defaults. The three that matter most: http_requests_total — a counter of every request, labelled by handler (your endpoint), status and method . http_request_duration_seconds — a histogram of how long requests take, in buckets. This is where response-time percentiles come from. http_request_size_bytes and http_response_size_bytes — request and response sizes. One gotcha to learn now, because it bites everyone: the status label is grouped . After hitting /boom , the counter reads http_requests_total{handler="/boom", status="5xx"} — there is no status="500" series. Remember that when we write queries in Step 6, and again in the Traps section at the end. The duration histogram's default buckets are le = 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, +Inf seconds. A percentile computed from a histogram is an interpolated estimate inside a bucket, not an exact measurement — keep that in mind when we read "0.975 seconds" in Step 9: it is the honest estimate the buckets support, and widening the buckets is how you trade precision for cost. Step 5 — Point Prometheus at the app Prometheus pulls metrics: every few seconds it fetches /metrics and stores the numbers as time series. Create prometheus.yml : global : scrape_interval : 5s # a demo choice — the default is 1m scrape_configs : - job_name : fastapi static_configs : - targets : [ "localhost:8000" ] The 5-second scrape interval is a deliberate demo choice so the dashboard moves while you watch; in production, 15–60 seconds is normal. Start Prometheus with this config ( ./prometheus --config.file=prometheus.yml from the folder you extracted it to), then open http://localhost:9090/targets : the fastapi target must read UP . If it reads DOWN, stop and fix that first — every later step depends on it (see Traps). Step 6 — Ask three questions with PromQL Monitoring dashboards are built from three questions — the RED method : Rate (how much traffic am I getting?), Errors (how much of it is failing?), Duration (how slow is it?). Each one is a single Prometheus query. Try them in Prometheus's own graph tab first ( http://localhost:9090/graph ). Rate — requests per second, per endpoint. rate(...) turns the ever-growing counter into a per-second rate over a window — here, the last 5 minutes: sum by (handler) (rate(http_requests_total{handler! = "/metrics" , handler != "none" } [ 5m ] ) ) Errors — the share of responses that are 5xx. Note the grouped label from Step 4: the numerator selects status="5xx" , because status="500" does not exist: sum(rate(http_requests_total{status = "5xx" } [ 5m ] ) ) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{handler! = "/metrics" } [ 5m ] ) ) Duration — the 95th percentile response time, per endpoint. Read it as: "95% of requests were faster than this." histogram_quantile does the bucket interpolation for you: histogram_quantile ( 0.95 , sum by (handler, le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{handler! = "/metrics" , handler != "none" } [ 5m ] ) ) ) Step 7 — Connect Grafana to Prometheus Start Grafana (run the grafana server binary from the folder you extracted it to) and sign in at http://localhost:3000 (the first-run login is admin / admin ). Go to Connections → Data sources → Add data source → Prometheus , and set the URL to http://localhost:9090 : Click Save & test . You want the green confirmation that Grafana successfully queried the Prometheus API — that message is the whole step done: Running Grafana in Docker instead? Then localhost is the container, not your machine — use host.docker.internal in the URL. This is the single most common reason a first data source fails its test (see Traps). Step 8 — Build the RED dashboard Create a dashboard with three panels — one per question from Step 6, using the same three queries: Rate — requests/sec by handler (the rate query) Errors — share of 5xx responses (the errors query; set the unit to percent 0–1) Duration — p95 and p50 by handler (the duration query, plus the same query at 0.50) Set the dashboard to refresh every 5 seconds and show the last 15 minutes. Send some gentle traffic to the app and you should see the baseline: about a request a second, a small 5xx share from /boom , and the Duration panel already telling a story — /slow sits up near a second while everything else hugs the floor. Step 9 — The burst: watch it catch a slow endpoint live Now attack your own app. The companion repository's load_burst.py runs a four-phase load timeline — baseline, an all-endpoints burst, a slow-heavy phase, then an error-heavy phase. The full run made 2,285 requests : 1,767 to / , 344 to /slow , and 174 to /boom (every one an HTTP 500). What the dashboard showed, in order: Rate climbed first — peaking at roughly 19 requests per second measured on a 2-minute window. (Your dashboard's 5-minute window will show a lower peak, around 6 req/s. Both are correct — a rate is meaningless without its window, which is why this post states the window every time.) Errors followed — at the peak of the error-heavy phase, over 11% of responses were failing (11.4% measured). Duration is the tell. /slow 's p95 read 0.975 seconds — and it had read that since the very first scrape, long before the burst, because the endpoint sleeps 0.8 seconds and the histogram interpolates inside its 0.5–1.0 bucket. The dashboard did not just catch the burst; it had already fingered the slow endpoint at baseline. (The overall p95 across all endpoints peaked at about 0.90 seconds during the burst — remember that number when we set the alert threshold in Step 10.) Step 10 — One alert: know when it happens again A dashboard you must watch is a chore; an alert watches for you. In Grafana: Alerting → Alert rules → New alert rule . Query the overall p95 (the duration query without the per-handler split), and set the condition: when the last value of that query is above 0.5 , sustained for 1 minute : Run the burst again and wait. Once the p95 stays above half a second for a full minute, the rule flips to Firing : Two honest notes. First, this demo wires no notification channel — the rule fires in Grafana's UI, and connecting email, Slack or a webhook (a "contact point") is your next step; this post does not claim a message was delivered. Second, the same rule exists as a Prometheus alerting rule in YAML in the companion repository, for setups that alert from Prometheus instead of Grafana. Traps (each one cost somebody an hour) Target DOWN. If Prometheus shows your target as DOWN, nothing else can work. Usually the app is not running, or the port in prometheus.yml is wrong. Check Targets before debugging queries. Docker networking. If Grafana runs in Docker and Prometheus (or the app) runs on your host, localhost inside the data-source URL points at the container. Use host.docker.internal . Querying status="500" . It returns an empty result — not an error, just nothing — because the instrumentator groups statuses ( 5xx ). An empty graph here almost always means a label value that does not exist, not "no errors". Recap You now have the full loop: the app publishes its own numbers at /metrics (two calls to add), Prometheus scrapes them every few seconds, three PromQL queries answer Rate, Errors and Duration, a Grafana dashboard shows them live, and one alert fires when the p95 stays too high. The pattern transfers unchanged to a real application: keep the three questions, watch the labels (grouped statuses!), and always quote a rate with its window. Practice task: add the instrumentator to an app of your own, find your slowest endpoint's p95 at baseline, and write the number down. If it surprises you, the dashboard has already paid for itself. FAQ Do I need Docker for Prometheus and Grafana? No. Both are single binaries that run locally, which is how this tutorial was produced. Docker works too — just mind the host.docker.internal note in Step 7. Why is my p95 an estimate? Because it comes from a histogram: Prometheus knows how many requests fell into each duration bucket, and histogram_quantile interpolates inside the bucket. It is the right tool for spotting slow endpoints, not a stopwatch. What does this cost to run in production? Prometheus and Grafana OSS are free and self-hosted. The real cost is storage, which you control with the scrape interval and retention settings — start at 15–60 second scrapes, not the 5 seconds this demo used. Sources prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator — PyPI project page (the instrumentator's defaults and label behaviour) Prometheus — Querying basics (rate, histogram_quantile, label matchers) Grafana — Alerting documentation (alert rules, conditions, pending/firing states) All measurements in this post (request counts, rates, percentiles, the firing alert) are from the author's own run of the companion code, November 2026. This post was originally published on Visual Studio Learn , where the video version and the free companion code are linked.

title: I built Aegis — a personal cyber defense platform that checks links, emails, files and passwords before they hurt you
author: Manoj Kumar Sharma
summary: Most people don't get hacked by nation-state attacks. They get hacked by a fake link in a text message, a convincing "verify your account" email, a malware attachment disguised as an invoice, or a password that already leaked in someone else's data breach. So I built Aegis — one place where a non-technical person can check each of those things before it hurts them, built to the same security standard it checks for. 🔗 Live demo: https://aegis-cyber-defense-platform.onrender.com (free hosting — first load after idle can take ~ a minute) 💻 Code: https://github.com/Manoj-2424150118/aegis-cyber-defense-platform What it does Smart Scan is the front door: paste anything — a link, an email, a suspicious message — and Aegis detects what it is and routes it to the right analyser automatically. Underneath are 10 tools , each answering a question a worried user actually asks: URL Analyser — "Is this link safe?" IP-instead-of-domain, look-alike domains, brand names hidden in paths, shorteners, credential bait. Email Analyser — "Is this email really from my bank?" SPF/DKIM/DMARC authentication, display-name mismatches, pressure language, and every link inside re-scored. File Scanner — "Is this attachment dangerous?" Content-vs-extension mismatches, double extensions like invoice.pdf.exe , hidden code. Files are examined in memory only — never opened, never run, never saved. Password Lab — offline guess-time estimation, common/repetitive pattern detection, secure generation. Breach Check — k-anonymity lookup: only the first five characters of the password's hash ever leave the machine. Secret Scanner — finds leaked API keys and credentials hiding in text and code. Encrypted Vault — AES-256-GCM with keys derived via Argon2id; the server stores only scrambled data, and tampering is detected automatically. Website Audit — any site graded A–F on HTTPS enforcement, security headers and cookie safety. Scam Message Checker — recognises Indian scam scripts: fake "digital arrest" threats, KYC/account-block warnings, OTP harvesting, Telegram task scams. Domain & TLS Checker — live grading of a domain's email-auth records, plus a real handshake to verify a site's certificate. The part most tools skip: the fix Every finding in every report ends with a Suggested Fix — concrete next steps written for the person holding the report. A test enforces that no finding can ship without one. A report should end the problem, not just name it. Since v2.0, a detection-engine "Signal" layer sits across the analysers, and public Trends show what people are actually checking. How it protects itself A security tool has to survive its own audit: The website-audit feature could once have been tricked into fetching internal network addresses (SSRF). It now resolves every target first, refuses private/internal addresses, and re-checks every redirect. Uploads are read in capped chunks and rejected exactly at the 10 MB limit — no memory-exhaustion via huge files. Login responses are timing-equalised with generic errors, so attackers can't enumerate real accounts. Accounts lock after repeated failures; login is rate-limited. Auth is Argon2id + JWT, and the platform ships the same strict security headers its own audit module grades other sites on. Aegis's self-audit score: 100, grade A . Testing is evidence, not decoration 186 automated tests , all passing, with CI and CodeQL green on every push. The canonical reference scores never drift between releases: the reference phishing link scores 85, the phishing email 100, the disguised program 40 — in every battery, on every version. A scripted QA battery (functional checks, attack suite, fuzzing, load) runs in a sandbox before deployment and against the live site after it. Stack FastAPI (Python) back end, React + TypeScript front end, single Docker container, Neon Postgres for storage (accounts and vault items survive redeploys — proven by test). Honest limits The demo runs on free hosting, which sleeps when idle — the first load can take about a minute. The code is identical to what a paid deployment would run. The checkers use explained heuristics, not magic. They can over- or under-flag at the margins — which is exactly why every finding shows its reasoning, so the user can judge. I'm Manoj Kumar Sharma, a cybersecurity & software professional (MCA, Manipal University Jaipur) based in Jaipur, India. I also run Scam Decoded , where I break down real Indian scams in short videos. If you try Aegis, I'd genuinely like to hear what it got right — and what it missed.

title: Three filters, cheap to expensive: how a duplicate finder avoids hashing your whole disk
author: alice kelly
summary: Every duplicate file finder starts with the same obvious plan: hash every file, group by digest. It is correct, it is simple, and on a real drive it is unusable. Here is the naive baseline, measured on a 1.09 GB working folder with 877 files: naive: 877 files, 1.09 GB, 21.2 s (SHA-256 over every byte) 21 seconds for one gigabyte. A 500 GB drive is three hours, and that is before you count the USB drive that spins down every 30 seconds. The fix is not a faster hash. SHA-256 is already fast enough — the CPU is not the bottleneck, the disk is. The fix is not reading the bytes at all for the files that cannot possibly be duplicates. Filter 1 — size (free) os.stat gives you the size without opening the file. Two files with different sizes are not duplicates, full stop. This filter costs one syscall per file and eliminates the majority of a normal folder. def _by_size ( self , entries ) : buckets = defaultdict ( list ) for e in entries : buckets [ e . size ] . append ( e ) return { s : v for s , v in buckets . items ( ) if len ( v ) > 1 } Only buckets with more than one member survive. On a typical disk that is a small fraction of the file count — photos, videos, and documents almost all have unique sizes. Filter 2 — the first 4 KB Files that share a size are the only candidates left. For those, read 4 KB and hash that. HEAD_BYTES = 4096 def _hash_file ( path , limit = None ) : h = hashlib . sha256 ( ) remaining = limit with open ( _long_path ( path ) , "rb" ) as f : while True : want = CHUNK if remaining is None else min ( CHUNK , remaining ) if want <= 0 : break chunk = f . read ( want ) if not chunk : break h . update ( chunk ) if remaining is not None : remaining -= len ( chunk ) return h . hexdigest ( ) 4 KB is not a magic number. It is the point where the cost of the read is negligible compared to opening the file at all, and where formats diverge: JPEG headers, ZIP local headers, MP4 ftyp boxes, and Office files all differ within the first few hundred bytes. Two files that agree on both size and first 4 KB are either duplicates or deliberately constructed to look like them. Filter 3 — full SHA-256, only for survivors Whatever is still standing gets read end to end and hashed properly. groups = defaultdict ( list ) for e in candidates : d = _hash_file ( e . path ) # full read groups [ d ] . append ( e ) The point of this stage is not speed. It is that this is the only stage allowed to decide a file gets deleted , and it uses a cryptographic digest, not CRC32, not a size match, not a filename pattern. Duplicate cleaners get one-star reviews for exactly one reason: they deleted something that was not a duplicate. What it actually measures Same folder, same machine, three filters instead of one: three-layer: 872 files seen, 279 hashed (32.0%), 42 groups, 107 duplicate files, 184.6 MB reclaimable, 9.9 s naive: 877 files, 21.2 s 2.1x on 1.09 GB. That number is unimpressive, and it is worth being honest about why: this folder is small and it is full of build artefacts that genuinely collide on size. The ratio is not a constant — it is a function of how much of your disk is unique. On a photo library where every file is a different size, filter 1 alone removes almost everything and the speedup is an order of magnitude. On a folder of copied installers it approaches 1x, because most of the data really is duplicate and really does have to be read. The metric that matters is not files hashed. It is bytes read , and filters 1 and 2 exist to make that number small. Two Windows traps that break the naive version Hard links. st_nlink > 1 means several names point at one inode. They are not duplicates — deleting either name frees nothing, because the data is still referenced. A finder that reports them as duplicates and "cleans" them gives the user a fake number and zero reclaimed space. key = ( st . st_dev , st . st_ino ) if st . st_nlink > 1 : if key in seen_inodes : continue seen_inodes . add ( key ) Long paths. MAX_PATH is 260 characters and open() fails past it. Prefixing with \\?\ bypasses the limit, but only for absolute paths, and only on Windows: if len ( s ) >= 240 and not s . startswith ( "\\\\" ) : return "\\\\?\\" + s The 240 threshold, not 260, leaves room for the prefix itself and for the path separator that gets appended. The shape of the whole thing walk → os.walk, prune excluded dirs in place, collect (path, size, inode) by size → keep only buckets with >1 member by head → 4 KB SHA-256 inside those buckets, keep only >1 full hash → SHA-256 end to end, that digest decides Four stages, about 40 lines of logic, and the expensive one runs on a third of the files or fewer. The same shape works for photo libraries, backups, and the Downloads folder everyone has been meaning to clean since 2019. FileDedupe is a Windows duplicate file finder that uses this pipeline. Free on the Microsoft Store . Code excerpts above are from the shipping scanner.

title: Dedupe a B2B Company List in Python Before Outreach: Root Domains, Phone Keys and Union-Find
author: MantisAI
summary: A prospect list merged from several sources usually contains the same company more than once. One row comes from a directory with https://www.shreepack.co.in/contact , another from a trade portal as shreepack.co.in with a sales email, and a third with only a Gmail address and a phone number written as 098290-12345 . If you send outreach from that list, the same owner gets three messages in a day, and that is the fastest way to look like a bot. This post shows how to dedupe a company list in Python with a small, standard-library-only script that collapses those rows into one company. It keys each row on a root domain and a phone key , then merges rows that share any key using union-find, so A matches B by domain and B matches C by phone and all three end up together. I tested every block below with Python 3.14; it needs 3.9 or newer for str.removeprefix . I work on Mantis, a prospecting tool for B2B teams. Duplicate rows are the first thing I clean in any merged list, and this is the approach I would hand to a developer starting from scratch. How to dedupe a company list in Python: the plan Input: a CSV with name, website, email, phone (any column can be empty) Output: one row per company, plus a merged_from count Rules: two rows are the same company if they share a root domain or a phone key, unless that key is shared by too many rows Save the blocks in order as dedupe.py . Step 1: imports and the lists that matter import csv import io import re from collections import Counter from urllib . parse import urlsplit # A few multi-label suffixes from the Public Suffix List. In production, # load the full list (publicsuffix.org/list/public_suffix_list.dat). MULTI_SUFFIXES = { "co.in" , "firm.in" , "net.in" , "org.in" , "gen.in" , "ind.in" , "co.uk" , "com.au" } # Hosts that never identify one company. NOT_A_COMPANY = { "gmail.com" , "yahoo.com" , "yahoo.co.in" , "outlook.com" , "hotmail.com" , "rediffmail.com" , "facebook.com" , "instagram.com" , "linktr.ee" , "wa.me" } # Platforms where each subdomain is a different business. TENANT_HOSTS = { "business.site" , "wixsite.com" , "blogspot.com" } Three small sets carry most of the correctness: MULTI_SUFFIXES : a public suffix is a name "under which Internet users can (or historically could) directly register names", and the examples given are com and co.uk. India has many of these: the Public Suffix List includes co.in, firm.in, gen.in, ind.in, net.in and org.in. I keep a handful inline to stay dependency-free; for real data, load the full list file. NOT_A_COMPANY : Gmail, Rediffmail, Facebook and Linktree never identify a single business. If you key on gmail.com , every sole trader in the file merges into one giant blob. TENANT_HOSTS : on hosts like business.site , the subdomain is the business, so the full host is the key. Step 2: root domain def root_domain ( value ) : """'https://WWW.Shop.Example.co.in/contact' -> 'example.co.in'.""" if not value : return None value = value . strip ( ) . lower ( ) if "@" in value and "/" not in value : # an email address value = value . rsplit ( "@" , 1 ) [ 1 ] if "//" not in value : # urlsplit needs '//' to find the host value = "//" + value host = urlsplit ( value ) . hostname if not host or "." not in host : return None labels = host . split ( "." ) if "." . join ( labels [ - 2 : ] ) in TENANT_HOSTS : return host . removeprefix ( "www." ) if "." . join ( labels [ - 2 : ] ) in MULTI_SUFFIXES : root = "." . join ( labels [ - 3 : ] ) else : root = "." . join ( labels [ - 2 : ] ) if root in NOT_A_COMPANY or host in NOT_A_COMPANY : return None return root Two traps here. First, urlsplit("shreepack.co.in").hostname returns None . The Python docs say urlsplit "recognizes a netloc only if it is properly introduced by '//'" and otherwise treats the input as a path. Prefixing // fixes bare domains without inventing a scheme. Second, the naive "last two labels" rule. Run it on www.shreepack.co.in and ops.acme.co.in and both come back as co.in . On an Indian list that one bug merges every .co.in company into a single record. The suffix check takes three labels instead. Step 3: a phone key (not a full phone cleaner) def phone_key ( value , country = "91" ) : """'+91 98290 12345', '098290-12345', '9829012345' -> '+919829012345'.""" if not value : return None raw = value . strip ( ) digits = re . sub ( r "\D" , "" , raw ) if raw . startswith ( "+" ) or digits . startswith ( "00" ) : digits = digits . lstrip ( "0" ) # already international else : if digits . startswith ( country ) and len ( digits ) > 10 : digits = digits [ len ( country ) : ] digits = country + digits . lstrip ( "0" ) # drop trunk prefix 0 if len ( digits ) < 10 : return None return "+" + digits This is only a matching key, not a validator. It strips formatting, drops the trunk prefix 0 used for STD dialling, and prefixes India's country code 91 so +91 98290 12345 , 098290-12345 and 9829012345 produce the same key. Short strings return None so they never match anything. My first version had a bug that the tests caught: it turned the UK number +44 20 7946 0958 into +91442079460958 , because it prefixed 91 to everything. Numbers that already start with + or 00 are now left as international. If your list is mostly one country, change the country default; if it is genuinely mixed, use a proper library such as phonenumbers for the key. Step 4: merge with union-find class UnionFind : def __init__ ( self ) : self . parent = { } def find ( self , x ) : self . parent . setdefault ( x , x ) while self . parent [ x ] != x : self . parent [ x ] = self . parent [ self . parent [ x ] ] x = self . parent [ x ] return x def union ( self , a , b ) : self . parent [ self . find ( a ) ] = self . find ( b ) def row_keys ( row ) : keys = { root_domain ( row . get ( "website" ) ) , root_domain ( row . get ( "email" ) ) , phone_key ( row . get ( "phone" ) ) } return keys - { None } def dedupe ( rows , max_rows_per_key = 5 ) : counts = Counter ( k for row in rows for k in row_keys ( row ) ) uf = UnionFind ( ) first_seen = { } for i , row in enumerate ( rows ) : uf . find ( i ) for key in row_keys ( row ) : if counts [ key ] > max_rows_per_key : # shared switchboard, agency domain... continue if key in first_seen : uf . union ( i , first_seen [ key ] ) else : first_seen [ key ] = i groups = { } for i in range ( len ( rows ) ) : groups . setdefault ( uf . find ( i ) , [ ] ) . append ( rows [ i ] ) return list ( groups . values ( ) ) Why union-find and not a groupby on domain? Because duplicates chain. Row 1 and row 2 share shreepack.co.in . Row 3 has only Gmail (ignored) and a phone number that matches row 1. A group-by on one column never joins row 3 to row 2; union-find does, because each shared key links two rows and the links are transitive. The max_rows_per_key cap is the part people skip. Some keys can be shared by many unrelated businesses: an accountant's number printed on clients' listings, a shared call centre, or an agency domain hosting many client pages. Without a cap, one such key glues dozens of companies together. In my test, seven rows sharing one number stayed seven separate groups with the default cap and collapsed into a single group when I raised it. Print the keys that hit the cap and look at them; they are usually worth a manual check. Step 5: merge each group and run it def merge ( group ) : """Keep the first non-empty value per column.""" out = { } for row in group : for col , val in row . items ( ) : if val and not out . get ( col ) : out [ col ] = val out [ "merged_from" ] = len ( group ) return out SAMPLE = """name,website,email,phone Shree Packaging,https://www.shreepack.co.in/contact,,+91 98290 12345 Shree Packaging Pvt Ltd,shreepack.co.in,sales@shreepack.co.in, Shri Packaging (Kota),,shreepack@gmail.com,098290-12345 Kota Steel Traders,http://kotasteel.in,,0744 2390011 Kota Steel,,info@kotasteel.in, Bharat Prints,https://www.facebook.com/bharatprints,,7742001122 Bharat Prints,,bharatprints@gmail.com,+91-77420-01122 Acme Logistics,acme.co.in,, Acme Logistics,https://ops.acme.co.in,, Nova Tiles,novatiles.business.site,,9001234567 """ if __name__ == "__main__" : rows = list ( csv . DictReader ( io . StringIO ( SAMPLE ) ) ) groups = dedupe ( rows ) print ( f "{len(rows)} rows -> {len(groups)} companies" ) for g in groups : m = merge ( g ) print ( f "{m['merged_from']}x {m['name']:<20} {m.get('website','') or '-':<38} {m.get('phone','') or '-'}" ) naive = lambda u : "." . join ( urlsplit ( "//" + u ) . hostname . split ( "." ) [ - 2 : ] ) print ( "naive:" , naive ( "www.shreepack.co.in" ) , naive ( "ops.acme.co.in" ) ) print ( root_domain ( "novatiles.business.site" ) , root_domain ( "shop.example.co.uk" ) , root_domain ( "example.co.in" ) , root_domain ( "x.y.example.in" ) ) print ( phone_key ( "0744 2390011" ) , phone_key ( "+91 98290 12345" ) , phone_key ( "12345" ) ) Output: 10 rows -> 5 companies 3x Shree Packaging https://www.shreepack.co.in/contact +91 98290 12345 2x Kota Steel Traders http://kotasteel.in 0744 2390011 2x Bharat Prints https://www.facebook.com/bharatprints 7742001122 2x Acme Logistics acme.co.in - 1x Nova Tiles novatiles.business.site 9001234567 naive: co.in co.in novatiles.business.site example.co.uk example.co.in example.in +917442390011 +919829012345 None The sample rows are made up, but each mirrors a pattern that shows up in merged exports. Ten rows became five companies. Shree Packaging merged through domain and phone, Bharat Prints merged through phone alone because both its Facebook URL and its Gmail were ignored, and the two Acme rows merged because ops.acme.co.in and acme.co.in share a root. What this does not do Fuzzy names. "Shree Packaging" and "Shri Packaging" are not compared at all; they merge here only because they share keys. Add name matching only as a tie-breaker inside a city, never as a key by itself, or two different "Sharma Traders" will merge. Chains and branches. Ten branches of one brand share a domain and will merge into one row. If you sell to branches, add the city or address to the domain key. Picking the best value. merge() keeps the first non-empty value. In production, prefer the most recently verified source. FAQ Why not just use pandas drop_duplicates ? It only removes exact matches on the columns you name. The rows above are never exact matches, and it cannot chain matches across columns. Should email domains count as company keys? Yes, once free-mail providers are excluded. A sales address at the company domain can be the only link between a directory row and a portal row. Is a phone match enough on its own? Usually, for small businesses, but that is exactly why the shared-key cap exists. Review anything that hits it. If you would rather start from a list that is already deduped, I wrote up how we build lead lists without buying databases here: how to get leads without buying lists .

title: I automated the monthly market brief I always wanted as an aerospace buyer.
author: Stephany Alves
summary: I spent four years buying aircraft parts, from propulsion components to avionics. Often, there was only one supplier to turn to, and I’d find out about a price increase when it landed in my inbox. Every month I had the same three questions before a negotiation: Is demand for these parts going up or down? Are supplier prices moving, and how fast? What is the exchange rate doing to my import cost? The answers exist, all of them public and free. They are just spread across three government sources that update on different days, in different formats, in two languages. So I built a pipeline that collects them, does the math and writes the one-page brief I wanted back then. It runs by itself on the 16th of every month. Repo: stephanyalves-eng/procurement-market-briefs What it produces Every edition has six one-page reports, each in English and Brazilian Portuguese, as HTML, PDF and PNG: Report Data Aerospace Supply Market Brief Public: Comex Stat, BLS PPI, Banco Central PTAX Brazil EV Supply Chain Brief Public: Comex Stat, import duty schedule Monthly Procurement Performance Report Synthetic buyer, indexed to public prices and FX Monthly Supplier Quality Report Synthetic EV plant Six Sigma Supplier Quality Report Synthetic EV plant Supplier Non-Conformance Report Synthetic EV plant The synthetic ones are labeled as synthetic on the page and in the README. More on how they are built below, because that part turned out to be the most interesting problem. Each page answers one sourcing question and ends with actions. The November edition opened with: aircraft parts imports up 11.1%, avionics producer prices up 17.2%, and a sharp BRL selloff raising import costs. A buyer can read that in ten seconds and walk into a meeting with it. How it works The flow has four steps: Fetch. pipeline/fetch_public.py downloads PTAX and IPCA from the Banco Central do Brasil, producer price indexes from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and import statistics by NCM code from Comex Stat. Extend the synthetic data. pipeline/synthetic.py appends the new month to a fictitious buyer's purchase orders, RFQs and quality notifications. Build. One Python module per report computes the metrics, draws the charts with matplotlib and writes the text. Playwright renders each page to an A4 PDF. Publish. A GitHub Actions workflow commits the new edition and attaches it as an artifact. Three decisions made the difference between a script that works once and a pipeline that runs every month without me. 1. The schedule follows the data, not the calendar The first instinct is to run on the 1st. That would publish stale numbers, because the sources release on different days. Comex Stat publishes the previous month early in the month, and the BLS releases the PPI around mid-month. So the workflow runs on the 16th, after both are out: on : schedule : # 16th of every month, 11:23 UTC (08:23 in Brasília) - cron : "23 11 16 * *" workflow_dispatch : The Comex Stat API only accepts a few requests per minute, so the client waits between calls and backs off on errors. That is why the job has a 90 minute timeout: the download alone takes 10 to 30 minutes. Every source also fails soft. If one API is down, the pipeline keeps the last file it has, finishes the edition and records the problem: for name in SOURCES : try : SOURCES [ name ] ( end ) except Exception as e : failed . append ( name ) log ( f "WARNING {name} failed, keeping the previous file: {e}" ) The page then states how far each source goes, so a reader never mistakes old data for new data. In procurement, a brief that silently shows last month's exchange rate is worse than no brief. 2. The headline is computed, not written This is the part I like most. A monthly report with a fixed sentence like "prices increased" is wrong the first month prices fall. So every headline, highlight and action is built from the numbers and changes wording when the data changes direction: up = k [ "g" ] >= 0 h1 = f "Aircraft parts demand {'up' if up else 'down'} {abs(g):.1f}% " \ f "and avionics prices {'up' if av >= 0 else 'down'} {abs(av):.1f}%" if fx_event and fx_event [ "chg" ] > 0 : h2 = ", while a sharp BRL selloff raises import costs" elif k [ "vs" ] < - 2 : h2 = f ", with the BRL still {abs(k['vs']):.0f}% stronger than a year ago" elif k [ "vs" ] > 2 : h2 = f ", and a BRL {k['vs']:.0f}% weaker than a year ago adds to import costs" else : h2 = ", with the BRL back near last year's level" (Simplified from briefs/aerospace.py , which also builds the Portuguese version in the same step.) The same idea handles layout. Long text would push a page past one A4 sheet, so render_fit renders the page, measures its height and tightens spacing step by step until it fits in 1123 px. The edition manifest records which level each page needed, which tells me when a text should be edited instead of squeezed. 3. Synthetic data that cannot see the future Real purchase order data is confidential, so the procurement and quality reports run on a fictitious company. The hard part was not generating fake rows. It was making a dataset that behaves like a real ERP export month after month. A real buyer looking at open orders on October 31 does not know which ones will arrive late in November. If the generator just created each month's data fresh, late deliveries would appear out of nowhere and the trend lines would jump. So the dataset has two layers: Truth tables hold every record with its real future dates: when an order will actually arrive, when a quality notification will actually close. The view is what a buyer would see on the cutoff date. Future receipts stay blank and open notifications stay open. def view ( cutoff ) : """Tables as a buyer would see them on the cutoff date.""" c = cutoff . isoformat ( ) P = P [ P . data_pedido <= c ] . copy ( ) P [ "data_recebimento" ] = np . where ( P . receb_real <= c , P . receb_real , "" ) . . . Two more rules keep it honest over time. Each new month is generated with a random seed derived from its own dates, so any edition can be rebuilt exactly. And extending the data only appends days after the last generated date; it never rewrites a past record. October's report does not change because November was generated. Prices in the synthetic orders are not random either. Each part category is indexed to the real BLS PPI series for its industry, and the currency conversion uses the real monthly PTAX. The company is fake, but its costs move with the real market. How I built it I developed this with AI pair programming (Claude). The split matters, so here it is plainly: the business questions, the choice of sources and metrics, the data logic (including the truth and view design for the synthetic data) and the review of every number are mine. The AI wrote much of the code with me and sped up the parts I am still learning. For someone coming from procurement into data, that is the honest way to work: I know which question a buyer needs answered and how to check that the answer is right, and the AI closes the gap between that and running code. What I would do differently Headline templates grow fast. Every new condition multiplies the branches I have to keep consistent in two languages. A small rules table would scale better than nested if statements. One run a month hides problems. A dry run a few days before the 16th, with --skip-fetch , would catch layout or data issues before the real edition. Monthly data is the ceiling. The PTAX is daily, but Comex Stat and the PPI are monthly, so the brief cannot react faster than its slowest source. Try it pip install -r requirements.txt python -m playwright install chromium python run_edition.py --skip-fetch # rebuild from the data in the repo You will want a free BLS_API_KEY for fresh downloads, since anonymous BLS requests have a low daily limit. If you work in procurement, supply chain or data, what’s one question you find yourself answering by hand every month? I’d love to hear about it in the comments. And if you’ve had a look at the code, I’d appreciate your thoughts, especially on how the synthetic data is put together.

title: 8 nutrition APIs compared: Nutritionix, Edamam, Spoonacular, USDA and more (I run one of them)
author: Tosh Koevoets
summary: I run Your Move, which includes a nutrition API. Disclosure done. I spent a year wiring food databases into a trainer app before we built our own, so I have been a paying customer of half this list. Our data is public and free: USDA FoodData Central and Open Food Facts. We structured it, removed the wrong entries and update it regularly, but we do not think it is fair to charge a lot for data that was free to begin with. So it is $19 a month with unlimited food searches and barcode scans. A large medical company that makes insulin pumps recently called us because fatsecret was raising its pricing a lot. They told us our data quality was on the same level, and we told them the $19 plan was enough. The three questions that matter: where does the food data come from, can you look up a barcode, and can you sign up without a sales call. Everything else is detail. The 8, side by side API Data sources Pricing Self-serve Barcode AI food logging Recipes included Your Move USDA FoodData Central + Open Food Facts, 3M+ products, 180+ countries $19/mo, 7-day trial Yes Yes Yes (text, photo, audio; Pro plan) Yes Edamam Own database, ~900k foods $9 to $58+/mo per product Yes Yes Yes Separate product USDA FoodData Central US government reference data Free Yes No No No fatsecret Own database, broad international coverage Contract (Premier tier) No Yes Yes No Nutritionix Own database, strong on US restaurant chains Custom (enterprise) No Yes Yes No Open Food Facts Community database, global barcodes Free (ODbL license) Yes Yes No No Spoonacular Own database, recipe-first From $5/mo, points-based Yes No No Yes API Ninjas (Nutrition) Not disclosed Subscription, full nutrients on premium Yes No No No Checked November 2026. Pricing pages move, verify before you commit. How I would pick You need to ship a food logger this quarter. Your Move or Edamam. Both are self-serve with barcode lookup and text-to-nutrition. Edamam bills per product, so nutrition analysis plus food database plus recipes is three subscriptions. Your Move is one key for all of it, including the exercise API if you ever need it. US restaurant menus are the core of your app. Nutritionix. Nobody else has that chain menu data. Budget for a sales conversation. International packaged foods. Your Move or fatsecret. Both have broad branded coverage across countries, and ours matches theirs. The difference is how you buy: fatsecret is contract only, Your Move is self-serve at $19. Budget is zero and you can build the product layer yourself. USDA FoodData Central for US generic foods, Open Food Facts for barcodes. Both are excellent raw data. Neither gives you serving sizes that just work, deduplication, or a search ranking a user would tolerate. That layer is what you pay the others for. Recipes first, nutrition second. Spoonacular. Its food ontology is genuinely good. Its nutrition data is a side dish. What a nutrition response looks like const headers = { 'X-API-Key' : process . env . YMOVE_KEY } ; const base = 'https://exercise-api.ymove.app/api/v2' ; // search, normalized per 100g so values are comparable const foods = await fetch ( `${base}/foods?query=chicken%20breast&per=100g` , { headers } ) . then ( r => r . json ( ) ) ; // barcode, with the country so you get the local label const product = await fetch ( `${base}/foods/barcode/041631000564?country=NL` , { headers } ) . then ( r => r . json ( ) ) ; // free text to logged meal (Pro plan) const meal = await fetch ( `${base}/foods/log/text` , { method : 'POST' , headers : { . . . headers , 'Content-Type' : 'application/json' } , body : JSON . stringify ( { text : 'grilled chicken with rice and broccoli' } ) , } ) . then ( r => r . json ( ) ) ; Three things I learned the hard way Ask where the calories come from. Several "nutrition APIs" are a thin wrapper over USDA with a markup. That is fine, but you should know, because then you also know what they cannot have: branded products and non-US foods. Barcode coverage is regional. A database that is great in the US can be empty in Brazil or India. Test with ten barcodes from your actual market before you sign anything. Serving sizes break more apps than missing foods do. Make sure every food comes with gram weights for its household units, or you will be writing a conversion table yourself at 2am. The full comparison with sources and a decision table is here: https://ymove.app/nutrition-api/top-nutrition-apis Wrong about your API? Comment and I will correct it.

title: Building HelpBLESS: A Help Board Works When Offers Are as Visible as Requests — What Worked, What Broke
author: OneLifeVibe
summary: Most community help software starts with a request form. Someone needs a ride to an appointment, a hand moving a sofa, an hour with a confusing form — and the interface asks them to describe the need, categorise it, and wait. Building HelpBLESS, a board where neighbours post what they need and what they can give, the request-first shape turned out to be a design bug hiding in plain sight. A board that only shows requests quietly teaches everyone who lands on it that asking is the only move available. The supply side of the community — the tools people would lend, the skills they would happily spend an hour on — stays invisible, so it stays unused. What worked Rendering offers at the same size as requests. An offer to lend a ladder, proofread a CV, or watch a neighbour's child for an hour is not a reply to anyone. It is a standing invitation, and it changes the next visitor's behaviour: a person who would never have posted a cold request will answer a visible offer, because answering feels like accepting help rather than admitting need. In matching-system terms, publishing the supply side first lowered the cost of the demand side showing up at all. Letting offers stay standing until they are taken. A request usually expires by embarrassment — it sits unanswered and the asker quietly gives up. An offer behaves differently: it can wait without losing dignity. Keeping offers up until the help actually happens meant the board accumulated a visible inventory of goodwill instead of a graveyard of unanswered asks, and each new request arrived to find plausible matches already listed. Showing follow-through in public. When an offer is taken up, the thread shows it. When a request is met, it closes where everyone can see. That record does more for trust than any onboarding copy, because a neighbourhood judges a system by finished exchanges, not announcements. It is the same reason a changelog beats a roadmap: evidence of completion is the feature. HelpBLESS is built around that two-sided board: needs and offers posted side by side, free to join and free to post, with help in the form of money, time, skills or advice, and posts that stay up until the help happens. What broke The request-only feed. The earliest layout led with newest requests, on the theory that urgency should sort the board. It sorted it into a wall of need that made the community look emptier than it was — prospective helpers scrolled past problems they could not solve and never saw the ones they could. The fix was not a better ranking algorithm; it was admitting the feed had been modelling only half the system. Categories designed for requests only. The taxonomy had tidy boxes for needs and nowhere natural for an offer to live, so offers got squeezed into request-shaped forms with the verbs reversed. Any data model that treats one side of a marketplace as the real entity and the other as a comment on it will eventually distort both. Offers needed to be first-class records with their own fields: what, where, when, and how long the offer stands. Expiry by default. Auto-expiring posts after a fixed window looked like tidiness and behaved like amnesia. Help boards are not news feeds; an unanswered offer from three weeks ago is often exactly the thing a new problem needs. Removing the silent expiry — and replacing it with an explicit "this happened" close — kept the board's memory intact. Lessons worth keeping A two-sided system is only two-sided if both sides are equally visible, equally structured, and equally allowed to wait. Requests are easy to design for because they arrive with urgency built in. Offers need the deliberate design work: first-class data, equal visual weight, and a public record when they land. Generosity that is easy to find gets used, and help that gets used gets repeated. Where have you seen a marketplace or community tool fail because only one side of it was designed as real?

title: Google PageSpeed Insights: How to Fix Critical Request Chains & Core Web Vitals
author: Mykhail Azhyshchev
summary: The B2B Performance Reality: Above is the actual diagnostic breakdown comparing a typical commercial B2B website against an engineered architecture. While SEO and accessibility often appear green in audits, Mobile Performance collapses to 34/100 because external font cascades create sequential network round-trips. For paid Google Ads clicks costing $20-$45+ CPC, every extra second of delay drives a 32% bounce surge before visitors ever see your headline. 📊 Benchmark: Slow Mobile Site (34/100) vs Optimized Engineering Core (99/100) Metric Typical B2B / Unoptimized (Live Audit) Engineered Target (azhyshchev.de) Business Impact Mobile Lighthouse Score 34 / 100 (Red) 99 / 100 (Green) +65 points Google Quality Score Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) 4.2s 1.4s -66% bounce surge Critical Request Chains 3-hop external font tree 0 Chains (Parallel WOFF2) 0ms render-blocking latency Google Ads Conversion Rate 0.8% 3.4% 4x lower customer acquisition cost The Paid Ad Problem Why Mobile Latency Silently Burns B2B Google Ads Budgets In high-intent B2B search campaigns, ad clicks are expensive. Keywords like "enterprise CRM migration", "AI automation consulting", or "invoice processing software" routinely command between €18 and €45 per click in Germany, the UK, and the US. Google Ads charges your credit card the millisecond the redirect occurs. If the visitor's mobile browser is connected over an average 4G or throttled cellular connection, the page has exactly 2.5 seconds to render meaningful content before bounce probability skyrockets. According to Google research, page load times increasing from 1s to 3s elevate bounce rates by 32%; at 5s, bounce likelihood jumps by 90%. When founders ask why their Google Ads landing page converts at 0.8% instead of 3.5%, the diagnosis is rarely the copywriting. In 8 out of 10 audits, the culprit is render-blocking latency caused by chained asset downloads. The Technical Bottleneck Anatomy of "Avoid Chaining Critical Requests" in Lighthouse When you run your URL through our free Mobile Speed & UX Checker or Google PageSpeed Insights, the most frequent diagnostic warning is: Avoid chaining critical requests — 2 chains found ( Max latency: 420 ms ) A critical request chain occurs when the browser cannot render text or images until resource A loads, which then discovers resource B, which in turn requests resource C. The most widespread offender is the default Google Fonts snippet: ⚡ Performance Architecture Comparison Phase ❌ Standard 2-Hop Chain (~580ms latency) ✅ 1-Hop Self-Hosted Fix (0ms blocking) **Hop 1** Browser requests HTML from origin Browser requests HTML with inlined critical CSS **Hop 2** Requests CSS from fonts.googleapis.com (DNS + TLS handshake) Fetches WOFF2 font directly via <link rel="preload"> in parallel **Hop 3** CSS discovers font binary at fonts.gstatic.com (2nd DNS + TLS) Reuses existing TLS connection over HTTP/2 **Result** **Blank screen** during all 3 sequential network round-trips **First Contentful Paint at 0.8s**, 99-100 Lighthouse score Step-by-Step Engineering Fix To eliminate critical request chains completely across your web stack: Self-Host WOFF2 Assets: Download the exact font weights your design requires in modern WOFF2 format. Store them in /fonts/ on your web server or CDN origin. Preload Above-the-Fold Fonts: In your <head> , issue a direct preload hint with crossorigin so the browser pipeline downloads the font before encountering stylesheet references: <link rel = "preload" href = "/fonts/jetbrains-mono-latin.woff2" as = "font" type = "font/woff2" crossorigin > Inline Critical Above-the-Fold CSS: Move layout, reset, and hero typography directly into a <style> tag in the HTML head. Avoid external render-blocking stylesheets for the initial viewport. Defer Non-Critical Scripts: Add defer and fetchpriority="low" to analytics, chat widgets, and social embeds to keep the main JavaScript thread completely unblocked (0ms Total Blocking Time). The 2026 Shift Why Fast Speed is Mandatory for Autonomous AI Agent Crawlers Speed is no longer merely a user experience or Google organic ranking factor. In 2026, autonomous AI search systems (PerplexityBot, ChatGPT Search, Claude Web Fetch, and WebMCP agents) crawl websites under tight operational budgets. Unlike desktop users who may wait 4 seconds, an AI agent runs synchronous HTTP requests with aggressive timeouts (frequently capped at 2.5 to 4.0 seconds total pipeline latency). If your server takes 800ms to respond (TTFB) and chains multiple external stylesheets, the AI crawler aborts the connection, classifies the domain as unresponsive, and answers the user's commercial prompt using your faster competitor's documentation. Sites scoring 95+ on Google PageSpeed with sub-1.5s Largest Contentful Paint consistently achieve higher indexing frequency across generative answer engines. FAQ Frequently Asked Questions ❓ How do I fix "Avoid chaining critical requests" in Google PageSpeed Insights? To eliminate critical request chains: 1) Self-host web fonts as local WOFF2 files and preload them with <link rel="preload"> instead of importing Google Fonts CSS. 2) Inline critical above-the-fold CSS directly into an HTML <style> tag. 3) Defer non-critical scripts with defer and fetchpriority="low". ❓ Why does a slow mobile landing page waste Google Ads spend? Potential buyers bounce before seeing your value proposition, directly burning ad spend. ❓ What is the difference between FCP and LCP in Core Web Vitals? First Contentful Paint (FCP) marks when the browser renders the first DOM element (text or logo, target < 1.8s). Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) marks when the primary hero block or main text finishes rendering (target < 2.5s). LCP is the primary user-perceived speed metric. ❓ How does website speed affect autonomous AI search agents?
