title: Modelling missing data: Sri Lanka's Grade 5 cut-off marks as typed tables
author: Hirantha Sandaruwan Lakshan
summary: Every year the Department of Examinations in Sri Lanka publishes district cut-off marks for the Grade 5 scholarship exam. The mark is out of 200, and it differs by district and by medium (Sinhala or Tamil). It is published as an image. I turned it into typed data for the Grade 5 scholarship cut-off marks page. Most of what I learned is not about exams. It is about hand-typed data that has holes in it. The shape: a record keyed by name, not an array The first decision was how to store 25 districts x 2 mediums x 3 years. A positional array is the obvious choice, and I rejected it. The comment at the top of grade5-cutoffs.ts says why: Keyed by district name, not positional arrays. This file is edited by hand once a year when the new sheet lands, and a value shifted one column in a positional array is exactly the kind of error a person cannot see. So the table is a Record keyed by district, with a tiny helper to keep each row on one line: export type Cutoff = { readonly si : number | null ; readonly ta : number | null } ; const c = ( si : number | null , ta : number | null ) : Cutoff => ( { si , ta } ) ; export const G5_CUTOFFS : Readonly < Record < G5Year , CutoffTable >> = { 2026 : { COLOMBO : c ( 139 , 135 ) , "NUWARA ELIYA" : c ( 133 , 132 ) , JAFFNA : c ( null , 133 ) , MANNAR : c ( 125 , 131 ) , // ...25 districts } , 2025 : { /* ... */ } , 2024 : { /* ... */ } , } ; The district list is a const tuple with satisfies readonly DistrictKey[] , and the year table is Record<G5District, Cutoff> . If I forget a district when typing next year's sheet, the compiler complains. A misspelt key fails the same way. A person squinting at a column of numbers would not notice either mistake. The type checker does. The three years sit in one object keyed by year. That is what lets the page show them side by side. The page indexes G5_CUTOFFS[year][district][medium] and nothing else, and the "vs previous year" column is the same lookup with year - 1 . null is not zero Some cells are empty. The Department published no Sinhala-medium cut-off for Jaffna in any of the three years, and none for Kilinochchi in 2024 and 2026. In 2025 Kilinochchi has 127. The Department has not said why, so the file stores null and says in a comment that "too few Sinhala-medium candidates" is only my own inference. The risk with null in JavaScript is how forgiving it is. Math.min(139, null) is 0 , because null coerces to zero. A "lowest district" fact computed naively would report a cut-off of 0. So g5Range in facts.ts filters first and keeps the count of what it actually used: export function g5Range ( year : G5Year , medium : Medium ) { const published = G5_DISTRICTS . flatMap ( ( d ) => { const v = G5_CUTOFFS [ year ] [ d ] [ medium ] ; return v === null ? [ ] : [ { d , v } ] ; } ) ; const min = Math . min ( . . . published . map ( ( p ) => p . v ) ) ; const max = Math . max ( . . . published . map ( ( p ) => p . v ) ) ; return { min , max , minDistricts : published . filter ( ( p ) => p . v === min ) . map ( ( p ) => p . d ) , maxDistricts : published . filter ( ( p ) => p . v === max ) . map ( ( p ) => p . d ) , published : published . length , } ; } I ran it against the real data. For 2026 Sinhala medium it returns min: 125 , max: 139 and published: 23 . It is 23 and not 25 because Jaffna and Kilinochchi are skipped. Tamil medium returns min: 130 , max: 135 , published: 25 . Note that it returns the list of districts at each end, not one district. Ties are normal in this data: nine districts share the 139 top band. A function that returned "the highest district" would pick one of them arbitrarily and the sentence built from it would be wrong. District names stored once, in three languages The page is available in English, Sinhala and Tamil. District names are the part where translation matters most, because a parent looks for their own district. The names are stored once, keyed by the same upper-case English key used in the cut-off table. The Sinhala and English labels come from a shared table that the university cut-off pages also use. The Tamil labels live in grade5-i18n.ts , because no other page needed them yet: const DISTRICT_TA : Record < DistrictKey , string > = { COLOMBO : "கொழும்பு" , "NUWARA ELIYA" : "நுவரெலியா" , JAFFNA : "யாழ்ப்பாணம்" , // ... } ; export function g5District ( key : DistrictKey , lang : G5Lang ) : string { return lang === "ta" ? DISTRICT_TA [ key ] : districtLabel ( key , lang ) ; } Because it is Record<DistrictKey, string> , a missing Tamil name is a compile error. Running it gives: en Nuwara Eliya Jaffna si නුවරඑළිය යාපනය ta நுவரெலியா யாழ்ப்பாணம் The data tables never contain a display name. Only the key is stored with the numbers, and the label is looked up at render time. Key facts are computed, not typed Under the page's intro there is a box of key facts. The header comment of facts.ts states the rule: nothing in it types a figure in. When a number in the table is corrected, the prose moves with it. grade5KeyFacts() builds sentences from g5Range , g5Unpublished and a reduce over the 12-year history: const lowest = history . reduce ( ( a , b ) => ( b . si < a . si ? b : a ) ) ; const peak = history . reduce ( ( a , b ) => ( b . si > a . si ? b : a ) ) ; Here is the output I got from running it: Across 25 districts the 2026 Sinhala-medium cut-off runs from 125 (Mannar, Vavuniya, Mullaitivu and Batticaloa) to 139, and the Tamil-medium cut-off from 130 (Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa) to 135. 139 is the lowest Sinhala-medium common cut-off in the 12 years from 2015 to 2026; the peak was 169 in 2020. The trend sentence has two templates. If the latest year is the lowest, it says so. Otherwise it says when the low was. That branch exists because "this is the lowest in 12 years" is only true until next year's sheet lands. A hard-coded sentence would go stale without anyone noticing. The facts file also gets a second check: a QA test recomputes the headline values a different way, to catch a bug in the facts code itself. Year-on-year change is the one thing the page does in the UI, not in facts.ts , but the principle is the same. Comparing the 2026 table with the 2025 table: District 2025 si / ta 2026 si / ta Colombo 140 / 134 139 / 135 Mannar 127 / 131 125 / 131 Anuradhapura 133 / 131 133 / 130 So Sinhala medium in Colombo fell by one mark while Tamil medium rose by one. The cut-offs for the two mediums do not move together. Honest limits No machine-readable source. The sheet is an image, so every cell is hand-transcribed. Each year's numbers were taken from at least two independent transcriptions that agree. One cell did not: Ampara, Tamil medium, 2025, was 131 in one transcription and 132 in two others. The file uses 132 and records the disagreement in a comment. Candidate counts are only partly checked. For 2024 and 2025 the per-district numbers come from the Department's statistical report, and I assert that they sum to its all-island totals. 2026's report was not out when I wrote the data. The "about 56,000 qualified" figure for 2026 comes from a single news report, so the type carries a qualifiedIsReported flag and the sentence says it is unconfirmed. Not covered. Cut-offs for individual schools at Grade 6 admission are not in this data file. They exist only as scanned tables, and I did not want to publish OCR guesses to parents as if they were facts. A cut-off is not a pass mark. A child on or above their district's cut-off is counted as qualified, which makes them eligible for the bursary and to apply for schools. The mark also changes from year to year, as the table above shows. What I would reuse If you keep a small dataset that people edit by hand, three things carry over. Key by name rather than position. Use null for "not published" and make every aggregate filter it explicitly. Generate the sentences from the data, with one template per case that could flip. How do you handle "no value" in your own datasets? Do you use null , a sentinel or a separate flag, and has it ever turned into a zero somewhere you did not expect? This article was written with the help of AI. The code, numbers and sources come from my own project and were checked against it before publishing.

title: Writing honest 'coming soon' placeholders instead of shipping fake features
author: Mobeen Ahmed
summary: Every tool site eventually has a feature that is not ready yet. On ramrom.io, that feature is Douyin. The download provider I looked at returns playlists, not files, so there is no honest way to offer a Douyin download today. I had three options: hide the platform entirely, ship a button that pretends to work, or put up a plain "coming soon" note. I chose the third, and I think it is the only one that respects the visitor. Why a fake button is the worst option A button that does nothing useful is not a placeholder, it is a lie. The visitor pastes their link, taps download, and waits. Then one of two things happens: either an error appears and the visitor assumes the whole site is broken, or the page pretends to work and the visitor waits for a file that will never arrive. Both outcomes cost trust, and trust is the only thing a free tool site really owns. I would rather a visitor left thinking "this site does not do Douyin yet" than "this site does not work". There is a second cost that is easier to miss. A dead button teaches me nothing. If the button is honest, I can watch how many people look for Douyin and decide whether it is worth buying a proper API. If the button is fake, the clicks it gets are meaningless, because some of them were people who would have bounced anyway once they found out it was fake. What an honest placeholder actually says My rule is simple: a placeholder must answer three questions in plain words. What is this? When will it be ready? What can you do instead? If it cannot answer the first one honestly, it does not go on the page. For Douyin, that looks like this: the card says Douyin, it says "coming soon", and it says the download is not available yet because no provider I have found returns real files for it. It links to nothing and it has no download button. There is no spinner, no fake progress bar, and no "try again later" message that implies the feature exists and is just having a bad day. A visitor who reads it knows exactly where they stand in about three seconds. The wording matters more than the design. "Coming soon" on its own is vague, so I add the reason in one short line. I do not write "we are working hard on it" when I am not actively working on it. The honest sentence is "not available yet" — boring, but true. The same rule applies to the code behind it An honest placeholder is also easier to maintain. The Douyin card is a static block of HTML with no JavaScript wired to it and no API call behind it. There is no disabled button pretending to be a feature, no endpoint that returns a fake error, and no half-built form waiting for someone to finish it. When the day comes that a real Douyin provider exists, I add the real tool. Until then, the page contains nothing I would have to rip out or apologise for. This is the same instinct behind the rest of the site. If a provider is down, the page says so instead of spinning forever. If a video is private or deleted, the message says that instead of blaming the visitor's link. The placeholder is just the same habit applied before a feature exists rather than after it breaks. The temptation to ship the fake version I understand why people ship fake buttons. A full-looking homepage feels more complete, and a grid with one greyed-out card feels unfinished. But the grid is not the product. The product is the download that actually works, and a visitor who uses the TikTok downloader successfully does not care that Douyin is greyed out. A visitor who taps a fake Douyin button and gets nothing will not come back to try the TikTok one. There is also a search engine angle, though it was not my main reason. A page that promises a feature and delivers an error is thin content. A page that says plainly what it does and does not do is a page I can stand behind when a reviewer reads it. My AdSense application was already rejected once for low value content, so I have learned to prefer honest, finished pages over pages that look bigger than they are. The checklist I use now Before any new platform or feature goes on the site, I ask four questions: Can I deliver the real result today, with a provider I have tested? If not, does the placeholder say so in plain words, with the reason? Is there a working alternative on the same page the visitor can use instead? Is there anything on the page that looks clickable but does nothing? If the answer to the fourth question is yes, the placeholder is not ready. A link that goes nowhere is worse than no link at all. Shipping less, honestly, has been one of the better decisions I made on this site. Visitors get a tool that does what it says, and I get a site I do not have to explain away. When Douyin becomes possible, I will build it properly and the placeholder will disappear. Until then, it stays honest.

title: Dubbing videos from Claude with an MCP server
author: Donatas Adomavičius
summary: I'm building Vocnu . It translates videos into other languages with an AI voice-over and subtitles. There's a web app and a Chrome extension for YouTube and course sites, and there's also an MCP server. This post is about that one: how to set it up and what happens when you ask Claude to dub a file. Setup You need Node 20 or newer, a Vocnu account (new accounts get 40 free credits, no card) and an API token from the app under Settings → API & MCP. The MCP server ships in the vocnu npm package, the same one as the CLI, so there's nothing extra to install. Claude Code: claude mcp add vocnu -e VOCNU_TOKEN = vocnu_... -- npx -y vocnu mcp Claude Desktop ( claude_desktop_config.json ), Cursor or any other MCP client: { "mcpServers" : { "vocnu" : { "command" : "npx" , "args" : [ "-y" , "vocnu" , "mcp" ] , "env" : { "VOCNU_TOKEN" : "vocnu_..." } } } } Using it After that you just ask something like: Dub ~/Videos/talk.mp4 into Spanish with Vocnu Claude uploads the file with vocnu_upload_media (up to 10 GB, uploading is free). It gets back the length, your balance and the price for each output and quality grade. The start tool asks it to confirm the price with you first, so nothing gets spent until you say ok or pick a cheaper grade. Then vocnu_start_job does the actual work: speech recognition, translation, a voice reading the translation where people talk, and the mix. The original audio is turned down, not removed, so music and background sounds stay. If you want it louder, quieter or off, just say so. vocnu_job_status shows progress and time left. When it's done, vocnu_download_results saves the files next to the original, or vocnu_share_job gives you a link that opens in a browser without an account. If a job fails or you cancel it ( vocnu_cancel_job ), the credits come back. A few details You can get the full video (MP4, MKV, MOV, WebM or AVI), only the voice-over audio, or only subtitles. Subtitles come with every output and can be burned in. There are SDH subtitles too, with sounds, speaker names and songs, for deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers. vocnu_voices lists the voices for a language with a short sample of each. So "use a calmer female voice" works, and Claude picks an actual voice id instead of guessing. Premium is the default. Standard and Economy are cheaper, with simpler voices and translation. For a lecture you only want to understand they're fine. If nobody talks in the video and the story is in on-screen captions, Vocnu reads the captions out instead. Without Claude npx vocnu login npx vocnu translate talk.mp4 --to es Same thing: it uploads, shows the price, asks before starting and saves the results next to the file. npx vocnu help has the rest ( --voice , --output , --burn-subtitles , --sdh and so on). Where MCP really helps is batches. "Dub the three newest videos in this folder into German and Polish and give me share links" is one message, Claude does the rest, and because of the price check it can't spend credits you didn't agree to. Docs are at vocnu.com/developers , the package is vocnu on npm . If you try it, let me know which languages or voices sound off.

title: Seven PreToolUse hooks cost 318 ms per tool call at 10 Claude Code sessions. One process got it to 89 ms.
author: Myeongseok Kang
summary: I run many Claude Code sessions on one machine at the same time, often ten or more. Each of them makes a shell call every few seconds, and every shell call goes through the PreToolUse hooks of claude-bulkhead , the plugin I wrote to stop those sessions from killing each other's dev servers, taking each other's ports and committing each other's half-finished edits. This post is about what those hooks cost, why the cost grew with the number of sessions, and how version 0.3.0 changed it. Where the time went Up to version 0.2, bulkhead registered seven separate Bash hooks: kill-guard, wait-guard, memory-guard, port-guard, checkout-guard, disk-guard and basics. Claude Code runs every matching hook for a tool call side by side, each as its own process with the payload on stdin. On an idle machine that looks cheap. The guards run in parallel, most of them only look at the command text, and one call took 47 ms on my MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, Node 24). The number that mattered was a different one. Starting Node alone takes 32 ms on that machine, so every guard paid most of its cost before reading a single byte of input. Seven guards meant seven Node processes per shell call. When ten sessions make a tool call at the same moment, which happens all the time when several agents are running test suites and builds, that is seventy Node processes starting at once and competing for the same cores. Each session then waited 318 ms for its hooks. With twenty sessions it was 611 ms. One process, cheapest checks first In 0.3.0 Claude Code starts a single hook for Bash and PowerShell, src/bash-guards.js , and that process runs the guards one after another. The order is deliberate. The guards that only parse the command text go first. The ones that may read git, the memory state, the process table or a port go last, and they only do that work after the text matched something: port-guard tries a TCP connection to the port before it reads any process list, checkout-guard runs git only when another session is alive, and basics runs git status only for git reset --hard and git clean . The process stops at the first block, so a blocked command never pays for the guards after it. The benchmark ships with the repository, so you can run it on your own machine: node scripts/bench-hooks.js 9 --sessions 10 On my machine it measured this: one process per guard (0.2) one process (0.3) one tool call, allowed 47 ms 76 ms 10 sessions at once 318 ms 89 ms 20 sessions at once 611 ms 109 ms The first row went the wrong way, and that is expected. Running the guards in a row is slower than running them side by side when nothing else is happening. I kept the change because nobody runs bulkhead for a single idle session. It exists for the case in the second and third rows, and there one process per call instead of seven is what keeps the hooks out of the way. Writing a block to the event log added no measurable time in either layout. What else is in 0.3.0 Merging the hooks also made two features easy that needed one place to see every guard's verdict. bulkhead explain -- <command> runs a command through every guard against the sessions, processes, ports and git tree on the machine right now, and prints what each one would say and why, without executing anything. Every block message now ends with a short code, and the user can run bulkhead allow <code> in their own terminal to let that exact command through once within ten minutes. A rule in basics blocks the agent from running bulkhead allow itself, so the approval stays with the person. kill-guard now also knows which session owns a process. kill <pid> and pkill -f <pattern> pass when they reach only your own session's processes and are blocked when they reach another live session's tree, and broad kills such as pkill -u , kill -1 , docker system prune and adb kill-server are blocked while another session is alive. The same guards can be registered for Codex, Gemini CLI, Copilot CLI, Cursor, Windsurf and five other agents with bulkhead setup <agent> --write . The full list is in the changelog . Trying it bulkhead has no dependencies and sends nothing off the machine. You can see what it would have done on your own history before turning anything on, because scan only reads your past transcripts: npx claude-bulkhead scan 30d To install it as a Claude Code plugin: /plugin marketplace add dooly6276/claude-bulkhead /plugin install bulkhead@bulkhead The code, the benchmark and the 18-second recording of a real session are on GitHub . Claude Code wrote most of the code and the tests with me, and I reviewed and measured every change described here.

title: Searching for a job in the AI era, part 2: where the AI got it wrong, and the real numbers
author: Giulio Calacoci
summary: Part 2 of a series. Part 1 covered the setup and the first 16 days. This post covers days 17 to 25 of my journey in search of a new job. I left you at the end of part one with the description of my setup and some numbers. Since then, I'm still jobless, but things seem to be moving somehow. As for the fun part, the tech one: I've discovered more things that the AI was getting wrong, I started using data properly, and I decided to burn more tokens of my Max subscription improving the overall workflow. Locations got misread, both ways I live in Florence and I would like to keep working remotely or somewhere near-ish. Because of this, the location filter matters more than any other, as it is the "first line of defence" against what I'm not interested in. The numbers I got from the first 2 weeks told me that about 40% of the roles I dropped failed on location. That number was big enough to make me want to look closer at it. The first question was: is there something worth saving in that 40%? A closer analysis showed that some misreads were happening during the filtering process. The first ones weren't even the AI's fault. Some job sources are aggregators (websites, Telegram channels, reposters...), and they confused the filters, letting some office jobs through. A posting in Florence, South Carolina, even got "confused" with Florence, Italy. The first set of fixes improved the filtering rules, so other Italian cities only pass if there is an explicit remote statement in the posting text. Hybrid postings get filtered out if they're not within a 20–30 minute car ride, and, most importantly, it's now clear that US Florence is not IT Florence. The worse misreads went the other way. The AI dropped postings, or parked them in limbo, because it misread where the company would hire. I noticed this because I kept checking postings myself during the job queue triage I run every morning. One day I went through nine of them by hand, checking each company's own application form to make sure that applying from Europe or Italy really was not an option. Three moved from limbo to the "to apply" queue because of AI misinterpretation. That was the part that worried me: we were dropping good jobs. The fix changed what counts as evidence. Before a location drop, a script now opens the company's own application form (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, etc.) and a cheap model looks for real rejection reasons. Only a restriction quoted from the company's own posting ("this position is open to UK only") or form can drop a posting. If the form can't be read, the posting comes to me with a note: "location check?". The next day, another three roles moved to "to apply" because their forms had no country gate anywhere. I honestly prefer to look at more postings than lose something good because a location is misinterpreted. Of the 31 postings checked by 8 November, 6 were dropped and 25 came to me, most because their form couldn't be read. Some got "saved", and I even applied to a couple of them. I read more, and I lose less. The sessions now argue with each other and improve my quality of life (and my CVs) I run several Claude Code sessions, each with its own area: the night pipeline, the triage, the applications. Since 7 November they review each other's work under written rules, and I approve the result. There is also a dedicated post for it . The goal was to simplify the flow and my life, providing a more refined result instead of forcing me to merge the conversations from multiple chats into a single mental thread. Additionally, some session scopes overlap, and each can benefit from the info stored in the other's context. In practice the output is better: each session has to convince the others, so what reaches me has more depth than what one session writes alone. On the job search, CVs, cover letters and form answers now go through one to four "council" review rounds on the applications that matter most. In the last few days those rounds caught errors that would confuse the recipient, claims my notes didn't back, and dates that contradicted my public CV. Let me be clear: as I said, I was reviewing every CV and cover letter "manually" or "humanly", but it's really easy to get tired or miss something when it's the fifth CV or letter you review. Context changes between them and you continuously go back and forth to check that the angle of the cover letter is correct or that the claims in the CV are actually useful. The council rounds made the result that was getting to me more refined, less prone to errors and in need of fewer changes on my side. Every claim still has to come from a file of facts about my work, which I write and correct myself. On 9 November alone I added nine new facts while preparing applications. The CVs themselves changed shape too, and the sessions argued that change through as well. Until last week my public CV followed the same two-page rules as the ones I send. Now the CV on this site is the long version: more space for roles, side projects, talks and skills, with no explicit page limit besides common sense, as no one wants to read a wall of text. It also acts as a template for every CV I send, keeping roles, section labels and dates, and only the content inside each section changes for the job. A reader who opens my site after reading a CV finds the same story, just less condensed. The method has already had its first outside "review" from a reader of the post on the council. The question was fair, and it turned into an improvement that recently went live in the council repository. The FAQ has the details. The night job is dead, long live the night job! The night job was a sequence of steps: scan, then judge what the scan found, then report. If one step broke, recovering required my intervention the next morning. I know. It was fragile. In my defence, I was sort of more interested in starting to apply to jobs than in making this more robust. Now the steps follow a producer/consumer pattern that lets the queues work at any time if something is ready to be processed. This also allows parallel processing of the queues, which is nice and speeds things up. If something is "wrong" in the queue, it's a non-blocking error: it just gets skipped and logged. This keeps things always on the move without losing anything. Everything runs every 30 minutes: not really "live processing", but it works for me. A comment on part 1 pointed me to ats-scrapers by kalil0321, an open-source project that publishes dumps of the postings on Greenhouse, Lever and Ashby. As I said earlier, postings can reach me through aggregators that cut the description and hide the company's own page. Now, when a posting comes from an aggregator, the judge looks it up in the dump and finds the original posting on the company's own job board (if available). The judge reads the real description, and the location check can read the company's form. On the first test, it found the company page for 120 of 634 postings. Thank you for the tip, commenter. The real numbers Part 1 said the scanner had made about 167,000 downloads. That number was honest but not useful: it counts the same posting again every night it's still open. From 31 October the scan also counts distinct postings. Part 1 (day 16) Now (day 25) Nights scanned 15 24 Postings downloaded ~167,000 323,570 Distinct postings (counted from 31 Oct) not counted 27,838 Kept by the script (title, location) 765 1,669 Read by me, after AI scoring 215 276 Applications 16 38, to 29 companies Replies (rejections included) not counted 12, from 9 companies Calls and interviews 1 5 Offers 0 0 For now, the data tell me that: Replies come fast or not at all. The median time to a first reply is 2 days. Two applications have had no answer after 21 days; 26 are still waiting. Many roles are old when I find them. The median posting was 31 days old when I applied, but I apply a median of 3 days after the scan finds it. Where the applications came from. Of 38 applications, 26 started on a company's own job board. Those 26 brought 7 replies and 4 of the 5 interviews. Location is still the main reason I drop a role : 42 of 117 drops, 36%. All of it runs inside my Claude Max plan; I pay no extra for the night jobs. Where my time goes The job review keeps getting faster, and the AI suggestions more reliable. That's my feeling at least, not a measurement, as nothing times it. Applying is the opposite, and it surprised me. I expected it to get quicker. Especially considering that there are posts around the internet on how to basically auto-apply to job boards. I timed 19 applications: the median was 62 minutes each (from opening the posting to pressing submit), from 12 to 111, and 18 hours in total. The slowest step is most often the same: my review of the CV and the cover letter, where new facts about my own work come up and the draft changes. The recent applications took longer, not shorter, because of letters, essays and review rounds. I hope the council saves me rewrites over time, but only time will tell. Applications are where I stay the gatekeeper. I said it in part 1 and it's still true: I want to be sure of what I'm applying to and how. The AI finds, filters, drafts and reviews. I review, fix, reject, decide, and ultimately I'm still the one who presses submit. Numbers as of 8 November 2026, day 25.

title: Same Template, Different Request: Fingerprint What You Actually Send to the Model
author: Obligra Verify
summary: An eval run drifts. You check the usual suspects: the model ID is pinned, the dataset hash matches, and the prompt template hasn't changed since last week's commit. Everything you recorded says the two runs were identical. They weren't. The gap is usually between what you versioned and what you sent. A template is an input to the request, not the request. Between the two sit a renderer, a JSON serializer, tool definitions built in code and whatever defaults your client library fills in. Any of them can change what the model receives without touching a file you hash. This post covers where those differences come from, a small way to fingerprint the request you actually send, and what a fingerprint can't tell you. Where "identical" requests differ None of these show up in a template diff: Key order. A tool schema built from a dict or struct can serialize its keys in a different order after a refactor or a port. Anthropic's prompt caching docs warn that some languages (they name Swift and Go) randomize key order during JSON conversion, which breaks caches. If the provider's cache sees two different prefixes, your logs shouldn't call them the same request. Whitespace. Python's json.dumps defaults to ", " and ": " separators, and indent adds newlines. A schema pasted into a system prompt as text carries that whitespace along. So does a trailing newline at the end of a template file. Defaults. A client library upgrade can change a parameter you never set. If you only log what you passed in, the record looks unchanged. Rendering inputs. Retrieved context, today's date, a feature flag inside the template. Same template, different text. template v12 ---+ retrieved docs -+--> render --> request body --> provider tool defs ------+ ^ | client defaults --------------------+ fingerprint the body, not "template v12" Fingerprint the effective request Hash the final request body, after rendering and after defaults are filled in, in a canonical form. Canonical means two JSON documents with the same content produce the same bytes, so the fingerprint changes when content changes, not when a serializer behaves differently. RFC 8785 , the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (Informational, June 2020), defines one way to do this: no whitespace between tokens, strict ECMAScript-style serialization of numbers and strings, and object properties sorted recursively while array order stays as it is. That last rule matters for LLM requests. Message order is meaning, so a canonicalizer must never sort arrays. Inside a single Python service, the standard library gets you most of the way. The json docs describe sort_keys as useful for regression tests, and separators=(",", ":") drops the whitespace. import hashlib import json def canonical ( obj ) -> bytes : # Close to RFC 8785 for typical request bodies, but not a full # JCS implementation (see the limits below). return json . dumps ( obj , sort_keys = True , separators = ( "," , ":" ) , ensure_ascii = False , allow_nan = False ) . encode ( ) def fingerprint ( body : dict ) -> str : return "sha256:" + hashlib . sha256 ( canonical ( body ) ) . hexdigest ( ) def send ( post , body : dict , template_version : str , log ) -> dict : resp = post ( body ) # hash exactly what was sent log ( { "request_fp" : fingerprint ( body ) , "template_version" : template_version , "requested_model" : body [ "model" ] , "response_model" : resp . get ( "model" ) } ) return resp Two tests pin down the behavior you want: def test_key_order_does_not_change_fingerprint ( ) : a = { "model" : "m-1" , "tools" : [ { "name" : "lookup" , "schema" : { "type" : "object" , "required" : [ "id" ] } } ] } b = { "tools" : [ { "schema" : { "required" : [ "id" ] , "type" : "object" } , "name" : "lookup" } ] , "model" : "m-1" } assert fingerprint ( a ) == fingerprint ( b ) def test_whitespace_inside_strings_does ( ) : a = { "model" : "m-1" , "system" : "Use the tools.\n" } b = { "model" : "m-1" , "system" : "Use the tools." } assert fingerprint ( a ) != fingerprint ( b ) The second test is the important one. Whitespace inside a string is content: the model receives it. Canonicalization removes serializer noise between JSON tokens, not differences in the text you send. If a stray newline keeps flipping your fingerprints, fix the renderer instead of hiding it in the hash. Compare in order when a run drifts Log the template version and the request fingerprint side by side, then check them in this order: Same fingerprint, different output. The request matched, so look at the provider side: model snapshot and run-to-run noise. Our earlier post on reproducible evals covers measuring that. Different fingerprint, same template version. Something between the template and the wire changed. Diff the stored canonical bodies. Different template version. Expected. That's a real change. Step 2 is only quick if you keep the canonical body, not just its hash. That body is prompt text, so it needs the same redaction and access rules as any prompt log. Limits Python's json isn't a full RFC 8785 implementation. JCS sorts keys by UTF-16 code units and formats numbers the ECMAScript way; Python sorts by code point and writes 1.0 where JCS writes 1 . If fingerprints must match across languages, use a JCS library on every side and test against shared vectors. A matching fingerprint means two request bodies were equal after canonicalization. It doesn't mean the provider ran the same weights, and it says nothing about whether the output was right. Defaults applied on the provider's side never appear in your body. Record the model the response reports, too. Where this fits Recording what an AI-assisted decision was actually based on is the problem we work on at Obligra. Obligra Verify™ is a system of record for AI-assisted decisions, in public preview, designed to retain the evidence your application selects. Its docs have a page on record integrity and verification , a related but different job: a request fingerprint tells you two requests matched, while an integrity check tells you a stored record hasn't changed since it was captured. Neither tells you the decision was correct. This article was generated by an AI agent (Claude) for the Obligra Verify team and checked against the linked sources.

title: 0 strings missing, still English on screen: taking a SwiftUI app to 12 languages
author: Bazi
summary: I make Alcove, a to-do list, planner and notes app for Mac, iPhone and iPad, written in SwiftUI. It is my own app, so read this as a build story, not a review. Version 1.4, out now on Mac, iPhone and iPad, added 11 languages to English: German, French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese (Brazil), Dutch, Japanese, Korean, Simplified and Traditional Chinese, and Hindi. Two things up front. The translations were made by AI: Claude, called from a Python script, then reviewed and polished by more Claude passes. No human native speaker has checked them. And the code was written with Claude as a coding partner (the commits carry its Co-Authored-By line). This post was written by an AI agent too, drafted from those commits. At one point the status command printed 0 missing in all 11 languages. At the same time, the screen of finished tasks was titled "OK" in French, buttons were still in English, and "Aujourd'hui" broke into "Aujo urd' hui". This post is about the gap between those two facts. The pipeline in brief There are eight String Catalogs: a Localizable.xcstrings for the Mac app, the iOS app, the widgets, the share extension and the TaskKit package, two InfoPlist.xcstrings for permission prompts, and AppShortcuts.xcstrings for Siri. Tools/i18n/sync-strings.sh builds both apps with SWIFT_EMIT_LOC_STRINGS=YES and merges what the compiler collected with xcstringstool sync . Today the catalogs hold 2,288 distinct keys between them. translate.py sends only the strings that lack a translation, in chunks of 60 by default, through the Message Batches API. Every request carries a glossary of 83 terms per language, which the model generated once and which every prompt then marks "use exactly". A few rows from glossary.json : { "de" : { "Quick add" : "Schnell hinzufügen" , "Inbox" : "Eingang" , "Pin (verb)" : "Fixieren" } , "fr" : { "Quick add" : "Ajout rapide" , "Done" : "OK" } , "ja" : { "Quick add" : "クイック追加" , "Due (as in \"Due today\")" : "期限" } } Every reply is checked before it is written back: the same format specifiers as the English ( %@ , %lld ), ${applicationName} as many times, no em-dashes. A string with one integer count must come back with one form per CLDR plural category: # CLDR also has "many" for fr/es/it/pt; it is left out on purpose, # Foundation falls back to "other", and generated "many" forms read oddly. PLURALS = { 'de' : [ 'one' , 'other' ] , 'fr' : [ 'one' , 'other' ] , 'ja' : [ 'other' ] , 'hi' : [ 'one' , 'other' ] , . . . } A failed row is retried once, then reported. Then a review pass made 297 corrections and a "native-speaker polish" pass made 2,784 rewrites. Both are Claude again; the polish prompt asks it to read as "a native speaker who uses an iPhone and Mac every day". A second review made 62 more corrections, and 148 long labels were shortened. Last, a blind audit: Claude, prompted as a strict native-speaker grader and not told the strings were machine translated, graded 50 random strings per language as 93.5% native, 6.4% acceptable and 0.2% wrong (one string, fixed). That is a model grading a model. My own notes say a native speaker's read is still worth having before calling any language perfect. translate.py status now said 0 missing everywhere. Here is what that number could not see. A word is not a meaning The screen of finished tasks is called "Done". So is the button that closes a sheet. Both used the same key: case . done : localized ( "Done" ) The glossary, rightly for a button, says "Done" is "OK" in French. So the finished-tasks screen in French and Spanish was titled "OK". The screen of tasks still to do, "Open", was German "Öffnen", the verb. An AI assistant's "Read" permission was "Vorlesen", which means reading aloud. Both AI review passes ran before this was fixed and kept all three, because a reviewer that sees only "Done" has no way to know which one it is. The fix is a key per meaning, with a note: case . open : String ( localized : "scope.open" , defaultValue : "Open" , bundle : . taskKit , comment : "Title of the screen of tasks still to do (open, not finished). An adjective, not the verb." ) translate.py hands that comment to the model as context. Now "Open" is "Offen" in German and "À faire" in French, and "Done" is "Erledigt" and "Terminées". The same pattern came back later: "View" on an attachment needed its own key, because the noun "Darstellung" is the Mac's View menu. And it runs the other way too: Dutch "Attach…" had come out as "Voeg toe…", the same words as "Add…". It is "Bijvoegen…" now. Text the compiler never extracted Text("Done") is collected by the compiler. Alcove's shared components are not so lucky: public struct PillButton : View { private let title : String public init ( _ title : String , style : PillStyle = . muted , . . . ) A literal passed to a plain String is shown as written, in English, in every language. The first finder, find-unlocalized.py , asked whether a literal's text was in some catalog. That had already led to about a thousand literals being wrapped. But "Tomorrow" was translated elsewhere, so this line passed: UpcomingRow ( task : TaskRowModel ( id : UUID ( ) , title : String ( localized : "Send the invoice" ) , priority : . high ) , day : "Tomorrow" ) , Screenshots of the phone in all 11 languages showed what was left. A UI test, LanguageShotsUITests , run once per language with xcodebuild ... -testLanguage de -testRegion DE , walks the main screens and attaches a picture of each. The new finder, find-unextracted.py , asks the compiler instead. Every literal that reached a localizing API is in a .stringsdata file with its file, line and column, so a user-facing literal at any other position is shown in English. About 500 more were wrapped. Then the Mac was photographed in all 12 languages and showed English that the phone pass and the finder had both missed: "+ New task", "On", the Settings title. The finder only looked at literals that start like a label, with a capital letter, so it learned about labels led by a symbol, "iCloud" or an emoji, and two-letter words. The App Store screenshots found four more, the Overview widget's lowercase captions ("today", "pending", "upcoming", "total"). Each pass found what the one before could not. Sentences built from pieces, and hand-made plurals This is how the delete warning for a list or folder was put together: let taskWords = tasks . count == 1 ? "task" : "\(tasks.count) tasks" case ( false , false ) : subject = "Its \(taskWords) \(tasks.count == 1 ? " is " : " are ")" // ... return "\(subject) deleted with it. \(undo)" No language can translate "is" without the rest of the sentence. Now each case is a whole sentence: gone = t == 1 ? String ( localized : "Its task is deleted with it." ) : String ( localized : "Its \(t) tasks are deleted with it." ) The selection bar did "Delete (count) (noun)s?". It is now a SelectionNoun enum with a whole sentence for each kind ("Delete (count) tasks?", "Delete (count) notes?"), because, as its doc comment says, other languages change more than an ending. The catalog holds the plurals (trimmed): "%lld tasks selected" : { "de" : { "variations" : { "plural" : { "one" : { "stringUnit" : { "value" : "%lld Aufgabe ausgewählt" } } , "other" : { "stringUnit" : { "value" : "%lld Aufgaben ausgewählt" } } } } } , "ja" : { "stringUnit" : { "value" : "%lld件のタスクを選択中" } } } English needs a "one" form too, or "(count) tasks selected" reads "1 tasks selected": translate.py asks the model for the singular of every count string, and 92 English strings have one now. merge-literals.py joins literals added across lines ( "first half " + "second half" ), so a sentence is one key. The day in Siri's confirmation, "on " + f.string(from: date) , became one string with a comment: "A due day in a spoken sentence". Layouts that broke in French and Dutch Longer words found every fixed width. In the Mac menu bar card, French and Dutch broke "Today" inside the word ("Aujo urd' hui"), and German broke the add button ("NEUE AUFGAB E"). The fix is to decide what gives way: // The weekday gives way first, then the title shrinks a little. ViewThatFits ( in : . horizontal ) { HStack ( alignment : . center , spacing : Space . md ) { Text ( "Today" ) . textStyle ( Typo . titleS , Theme . textPrimary ) . fixedSize ( ) Eyebrow ( environment . todayWeekday ) . fixedSize ( ) . padding ( . top , Space . xs ) } Text ( "Today" ) . textStyle ( Typo . titleS , Theme . textPrimary ) . lineLimit ( 1 ) . minimumScaleFactor ( 0.7 ) } In the footer, the links fold to symbols so the add button keeps its words. From the phone pass: the counter captions on Today ("ÉCHÉANCE AUJOURD'HUI") wrap at one shared height, priority chips shrink for "Dringend" or "अत्यावश्यक", and the meeting notes card stacks its two buttons with ViewThatFits when they do not fit side by side. The Overview widget's captions ran past their columns ("DEMNÄCH…"), and there the fix was shorter words: "bald", "du jour", "abiertas", "gepland", "abertas". Siri phrases and widgets Siri answers only the phrases in AppShortcuts.xcstrings , while Settings shows its own list of phrases from TaskKit. Translated separately, they would disagree. shortcut-phrases.py builds Siri's sets from the Settings list's translations, so a person in Germany is shown exactly the phrases Siri listens for. Each translation must name "Alcove" exactly once, and gets Siri's ${applicationName} token back. Two English phrases can come out as one. The code comment's example: "New task in" and "Create a task in" were both "Neue Aufgabe in". Siri needs each phrase once, so sets drop repeats, and English's ten ways to add a task are nine in German and eight in French. bundle-check.py , which reads the compiled tables inside the built apps and extensions, then had to hold a phrase set to being there, not to English's count. Widgets had their own English: the sample tasks in the widget gallery, "Tomorrow" in Upcoming, and the Overview captions, which got keys of their own because "today" and "total" are also words in other sentences. What I would do first next time Give every word that can mean two things its own key and a comment from day one. "Done", "Open", "Read", "View" and "Block" each cost a fix after translation. Write whole sentences with the count in them, never n == 1 ? "" : "s" or + . Make shared components' callers pass String(localized:) , and run the position-based finder before believing any "0 missing". Take screenshots of every screen in every language before the review passes, not after. Each round of pictures found English or broken layouts that the numbers did not. Get a native speaker to read it. AI graders gave these translations good marks, but that is not the same thing. One known limit stays: quick add reads English date words ("tomorrow", "every monday", !high ) in every language.
